verdictReason: Killed on edge and alternatives; payment is unproven. For vendors that publish OpenAPI specs, free open-source tools already diff, flag breaking changes and alert (oasdiff, openapi-changes, apibreak CI action), and the CC0 APIs.guru directory auto-updates a curated spec collection weekly with RSS, so curation is copyable in days. For HTML-only vendors, free page-change monitors (changedetection.io, hosted $8.99/mo) cover the alert. No page shows anyone paying $19/mo. Pessimistic cash +$91 on ~520 owner hours. Not verified: paid rivals' pricing pages, vendor ToS.

answers.question: (1) What free/cheap alternative covers the wedge?
answers.answer: For API vendors that publish a machine-readable spec (the large majority of the payments-style verticals the idea names): oasdiff is an Apache-2.0 'Command-line tool to compare and detect breaking changes in OpenAPI specs' whose changelog command lists changes 'breaking or not, in human-readable form', runs in CI via a GitHub Action and has a hosted layer at oasdiff.com (D1). pb33f's openapi-changes (Apache-2.0) is 'The world's most powerful OpenAPI breaking changes detector' (D3). apibreak (MIT) already targets the exact consumer-side job: 'Fails your CI build when a third-party API you actually call changes in a way that can break you', filtered to the endpoints you declare, free (D4). APIs.guru's openapi-directory (CC0) holds curated specs that are 'automatically updated from their original source' and offers RSS feeds for updated APIs (D2). Vendors such as Stripe publish their spec with a Releases changelog and Plaid a CHANGELOG.md in public repos (D6, D8). For vendors with only HTML changelogs: changedetection.io (Apache-2.0) 'Detect changes and monitor data in JSON API's' and alerts to email/Slack/webhook, self-hosted free or '$8.99/month subscription' hosted (D5). Case-file paid rivals (not re-verified): API Drift Alert $149+/mo (DEV-02-E1), Apify API Breaking Change Radar (DEV-02-E5), Deprecatr AI (DEV-02-E6). Gap left: severity-classified, per-field summaries of prose-only changelogs; no free tool read does that well, but a rival could add it.

answers.question: (2) What structural edge exists and who could copy it?
answers.answer: None found. The input is public (vendor specs, changelogs) and the output is a list of watched APIs plus a diff; no exclusive data, licence, network effect or switching cost. A rival can copy a vertical list quickly: APIs.guru already ingests specs weekly under CC0 (D2) and the diff/classify engines are open source (D1, D3, D4). Maintaining 30-50 vertical sources is labour, not an edge, and breaks whenever a vendor changes a page. What would falsify this conclusion: a vertical where the vendors publish no spec or changelog feed at all, curated sources that no tool covers, AND buyers visibly paying for it.

answers.question: (3) Who demonstrably pays and how much?
answers.answer: Nothing read shows a buyer paying for curated vertical API-change alerts. Price signals are: an idea site's opinion of $19-49/month that it calls a 'card-swipe decision' (DEV-02-E4, not observed purchasing), a $149/mo+ enterprise rival (DEV-02-E1, not re-verified), the generic page monitor's $8.99/month hosted subscription (D5), and an early-access project's proposed hosted tier of $49 per org per month, per WebFetch's summary of apibreak's README (not a verbatim quote; D4). Optic, an MIT-licensed OpenAPI diff tool, was archived by its owner on 2026-01-12 after Optic Labs joined Atlassian (D7), which says little about demand but shows no standalone paying base was visible. Case-file pain evidence (DEV-02-E2, E3) is blog posts from vendors of competing tools.

answers.question: (4) Legal and platform constraints?
answers.answer: Spec-based monitoring is low-risk: APIs.guru states definitions acquired from public sources fall under fair use and uses CC0 for contributed ones (D2); Stripe's spec is MIT (not quoted, per page summary) (D6). Scraping HTML changelogs and docs can breach vendor terms of service and robots rules (not checked per vendor; general knowledge). Prose changelogs have no stable format, so each source needs maintenance. Many vendors publish no OpenAPI spec (case-file note). No licence is needed to run the service; the entrant should avoid redistributing vendor docs verbatim.

answers.question: (5) Year-1 numbers?
answers.answer: Bottom-up (inputs are assumptions unless cited): price $19/month for 10 watched APIs; first revenue month 4 (reference entrant: day 90); 1.5 new payers per month with 10% monthly churn (alert-once users) gives ~52 customer-months; revenue365 about $994. Costs: small server and cron $10/month ($120), classification/LLM variable cost $1.90 per customer-month (the case-file estimate, ~$99), card fees 2.9% + $0.30 (~$44), domain $15; total about $279; base profit about $715, about $1.4 per owner hour over ~520 hours. Pessimistic (price x0.8, volume x0.5, cost x1.5): revenue about $397, cost about $306, profit about +$91, about $0.17 per hour, i.e. nominally positive but effectively zero return. Price anchor: changedetection.io hosted $8.99/month (D5).

killReasons.reason: For vendors that publish OpenAPI specs, free open-source tools already diff, separate breaking from non-breaking changes and alert the consumer (oasdiff, openapi-changes, apibreak, which targets exactly 'a third-party API you actually call'); the wedge reduces to who maintains the vendor list.

No exclusive or compounding edge: curation inputs are public and a CC0 directory already ingests specs 'automatically updated from their original source' at least weekly with RSS feeds; a rival can copy a 30-50 API vertical list in days and the engines are open source.

For vendors without specs the job is page-change detection, which free self-hosted and $8.99/month hosted monitors already cover for web pages and JSON; the entrant's added value (per-field severity from prose changelogs) needs LLM reading with unverified accuracy and ToS exposure.

No evidence anyone pays $19/month: price signals are an idea site's opinion, an enterprise rival at $149+, and a proposed hosted tier of an early-access project; the MIT-licensed Optic diff tool was archived in January 2026 (reason not stated).
Large vendors already publish their own specs and changelogs in public repos (Stripe Releases, Plaid CHANGELOG.md), so a free watch is the status quo for the biggest integration risks.

assumptions: Assumption: price $19/month for 10 watched APIs (case-file wedge price from an idea site, DEV-02-E4; no purchase observed).

Assumption: first revenue in month 4 (reference entrant: day 90); 1.5 new paying customers per month from month 4 and 10% monthly churn because many users need an alert only once; about 52 customer-months in year 1. No source supports the rate.

Assumption: server and cron $10/month ($120/year); LLM/classification variable cost $1.90 per customer-month (the case-file estimate, about $99); card fees 2.9% + $0.30 per charge (about $44); domain $15; total cash cost about $279.
Excluded: owner time (10 h/week, about 520 h; about $1.4/hour at base profit, about $0.17/hour pessimistic), time spent fixing breaking scrapers, legal review, and any marketing spend.

Pessimistic = price x0.8, volume x0.5, cost x1.5 applied to the base model: revenue about $397, cost about $306, profit about +$91. Nominally positive but effectively zero return on time, and it assumes the 1.5 payers/month base rate with no evidence.

legalNotes: Spec-based monitoring is low-risk: APIs.guru licenses contributed definitions CC0 and treats definitions acquired from public sources as fair use (D2, per page summary); check each vendor's spec licence before redistributing a spec.

Scraping vendor HTML changelogs or docs can breach website terms of service or robots rules (not checked per vendor; general knowledge); use only published feeds, specs and release pages and respect robots.
Alert text derived from vendor documentation should be summarised rather than copied verbatim to avoid copyright issues (general knowledge).
Many vendors publish no OpenAPI spec (case-file note), so a coverage promise to buyers needs careful wording and an SLA-free disclaimer.
unverified: Pricing and features of paid rivals (API Drift Alert, FlareCanary, Apify actor, Deprecatr AI, oasdiff.com hosted tier, ApiNotes): WebFetch to non-GitHub domains was refused (permission request unanswered) and WebSearch budget was exhausted, so DEV-02-E1..E6 were NOT re-checked.
Whether anyone pays for curated vertical API-change alerts at $19/month, and the true churn; no public page can settle this, the rivals' own customer/revenue data would.
Vendor-by-vendor ToS on scraping changelogs, and which healthcare, tax or shipping vendors publish no spec or feed.
apibreak's proposed $49 hosted tier comes from WebFetch's summary of its README, not a verbatim quote; Stripe MIT licence and APIs.guru fair-use wording are also from WebFetch summaries.
Quotes come from WebFetch's processed text of GitHub pages, not raw HTML; robots.txt blocked GitHub tree pages (skipped, not circumvented).
Why Optic was archived; it may reflect the Atlassian acquisition rather than weak demand.
